svg.aria-label: Diagram: the anatomy of a Google Cloud IAM allow policy binding, the union rule across the resource hierarchy, why a conditional role binding cannot narrow an unconditional one, and how reading a policy as version 1 discards conditions during read-modify-write
svg.title: Allow policies: one operation, addition — and a read path that drops what you wrote
svg.text: An allow policy has exactly one arithmetic operation: addition.
Nothing inside one subtracts. That single fact explains almost every confusing IAM outcome below.
A binding, and the metadata around it
principals (#31) + one role (#32) + optional condition
etag — changes on every update. Concurrency control.
An etag with no bindings grants no roles at all.
version — 1 has no conditions, 3 introduces them.
Version 2 is reserved for internal use, hence the gap.
The union rule
Effective policy = the policy on the resource UNION
the policies at every ancestor level above it.
Granted if ANY higher-level binding grants it.
Add a binding at any level and the access grant
scope increases. Never the reverse.
Consequence 1 — a condition cannot narrow a grant that is already unconditional
If the binding has no condition, the principal always has that role. Adding that same principal to a
conditional binding for the same role has no effect — it is another term in a union, not a restriction.
But a group present ONLY in the conditional binding does expire. One policy, both outcomes.
Consequence 2 — deleting the binding you can see often changes nothing
Removing a binding removes one term from a union, not the union. A folder or organization binding still
grants what you just deleted at the project. A revocation is unproven until the whole ancestry is checked.
Read-modify-write, hazard 1
Two systems read, both write, one set of changes
is silently lost.
Protected: send the etag back. A stale one fails
with 409 Conflict / ABORTED.
Retry the whole sequence, with backoff.
Read-modify-write, hazard 2
No version specified? IAM assumes version 1 —
which cannot express a condition.
The role comes back as ..._withcond_<hash> and
the condition itself is not present.
Protected by: nothing. No error is raised.
Which makes it a tooling problem, not a reading problem
The console and gcloud set the version for you, so nobody meets this interactively. It surfaces only in the
path that runs unattended, at scale — the side with the least supervision. Post #28, arriving in IAM.
Ask for requestedPolicyVersion 3. Grep your tooling for _withcond_ — if it appears, a condition was dropped.
Also: access changes are eventually consistent, so a returned write is the start of revocation, not the end of it.
And a recreated service account with the same name inherits nothing — the name is not the identity.
To subtract access at all, you need a different mechanism: deny policies, with their own evaluation order (#36).
